criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly describes prompt-regression mechanics - stratified/sliced evaluation, objective per-class metrics appropriate to classification+extraction, pinning a fixed model snapshot, the residual non-determinism of hosted LLMs even at temperature 0, paired statistical comparison (McNemar/bootstrap CI) to separate regression from noise, and prompt versioning by content hash. Deduct for incorrect claims such as 'temperature 0 guarantees deterministic output', 'aggregate accuracy is sufficient', or using BLEU/ROUGE for label matching.

Full marks require all five parts asked for - dataset construction/maintenance, deterministic harness, scoring with per-slice reporting, CI pass/fail gating with statistical treatment, and versioning/traceability/rollback - plus at least a nod to online guardrails. Both the rare-critical-slice concern and the noise-vs-real-regression concern must be addressed. Partial credit for missing parts.

Full marks: justifies the key choices rather than listing tools - why per-slice over aggregate, why a significance test/CI over a raw diff, why pin the model snapshot, why over-sample and grow the critical slice - and explicitly connects the design to how it would have caught the two `security_incident` regressions. Partial credit for asserted choices with thin justification.

Full marks: well organised, uses correct terminology precisely, and is concrete enough that a reviewer could implement the setup from the answer. Deduct for vague hand-waving, tool name-dropping without mechanism, or disorganised structure.

expected_answer_points: Maintain a curated, version-controlled golden/regression dataset stored alongside the prompt, stratified by category with the rare `security_incident` class deliberately over-sampled so a change on it is measurable
Grow the regression set from real production failures so each caught misroute becomes a permanent test case and the same bug cannot silently recur

Pin the exact model snapshot (not a floating alias) and use temperature 0/seed, while acknowledging hosted LLMs are not bit-exact deterministic - so run each case multiple times and reason over the distribution
Report and gate on per-slice metrics (per-class precision/recall/F1), not just aggregate accuracy, because a flat global number hid the collapsed rare slice - the exact reported failure

Use objective structured metrics (accuracy, per-class F1, exact/field match) suited to classification+extraction rather than fuzzy text-overlap metrics; if using LLM-as-judge, validate it against human labels and control its bias/non-determinism

Gate in CI by comparing candidate vs production prompt on the same data (paired), distinguishing real regression from sampling noise with a significance test or confidence interval and a tolerance band, gating hardest on the critical slice
Version prompts by content hash + semver and bind every eval run to a (prompt, model, dataset) triple for reproducibility, attribution, and one-click rollback
Complement offline gating with online guardrails (canary/shadow deploy, production distribution/confidence monitoring) that feed failures back into the dataset
common_pitfalls: Relies on a single aggregate accuracy/score and never breaks metrics out per class - missing the entire point that a 1% critical slice can collapse while the mean stays flat
Treats one eval run's score difference as ground truth: no repeated runs, no significance test or confidence interval, so sampling noise either masks a real regression or is mistaken for one
Assumes temperature 0 (or a seed) makes the hosted API fully deterministic, and/or forgets to pin the model snapshot - so a silent provider model update gets misattributed to the prompt change
Uses fuzzy text-overlap or embedding-similarity metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/cosine) for what is really a structured classification+extraction task where exact-match and per-class F1 are the right tools
Reaches for LLM-as-judge as the primary scorer without validating it against human labels or controlling judge bias/non-determinism, treating the judge score as objective truth

Equates prompt versioning with 'keep the string in code' - no content hash, registry, or binding of eval results to a (prompt, model, dataset) triple, so regressions can't be attributed or cleanly rolled back, and no feedback loop grows the regression set from production failures
reference_answer:
The reported failure - a wording change silently collapsing a rare-but-critical class while the aggregate metric stayed flat - is the canonical prompt-regression problem. The fix is a versioned, sliced, statistically honest offline eval that gates changes in CI, backed by online guardrails.

1) Evaluation dataset. Keep a curated, version-controlled golden set of (ticket -> expected category + expected fields), stored next to the prompt in git or a prompt/dataset registry (LangSmith, Langfuse, MLflow). Stratify it by category and deliberately over-sample `security_incident` so that slice has enough examples to measure a change at all - 20 tickets can't detect a recall drop. Grow it from production: every real misroute or caught regression becomes a permanent test case (a regression corpus), which is what stops the same bug recurring.

2) Harness & determinism. Pin the exact model snapshot (a dated model id), not a floating alias, so a silent provider model update can't be misattributed to your prompt. Use temperature 0 and a fixed seed where supported, but do not assume bit-exact determinism - hosted LLMs still vary from batching/hardware/floating point. So run each case k times and reason over the output distribution, not one sample. Identify each prompt by content hash + semver and log prompt-hash + model-id + dataset-version + results together for every run, so any result is reproducible and attributable.

3) Scoring & metrics. This is a classification+extraction task, so prefer objective metrics: per-class precision/recall/F1 for category and exact-match or field-level F1 for extracted fields - not BLEU/ROUGE/embedding similarity, which are noisy and wrong for labels. Crucially, report metrics per slice, not just the aggregate: the whole failure mode is a global number staying flat while one class collapses. For any genuinely open-ended sub-output, an LLM-as-judge with an explicit rubric is acceptable only if you validate the judge against human labels, curb its non-determinism, and watch for position/verbosity/self-preference bias.

4) Gating & statistics. In CI, run the candidate prompt against the current production prompt on the same dataset (a paired design). Because outputs are stochastic and the set is finite, a raw score difference can be noise: use a paired test (McNemar on per-item agree/disagree, or a bootstrap CI on the metric difference) and require the change to clear a tolerance band, not merely be numerically higher. Gate hardest on the critical slice - block the merge if `security_incident` recall drops beyond tolerance even when the mean improves. Size the slice for adequate statistical power and account for multiple comparisons across slices; flag flaky cases (varying across the k runs) rather than silently passing them.

5) Versioning & rollback. Prompts live in a registry/git keyed by content hash + semver, with each eval run bound to a (prompt, model, dataset) triple. That lets you attribute a regression to a specific change and roll back by repointing the registry at the previous version.

6) Beyond offline. Offline sets are always incomplete, so canary/shadow the new prompt on a traffic slice, monitor the production category distribution and model confidence, and feed failures back into the golden set.

How it catches the two regressions: per-slice recall on `security_incident`, measured on an over-sampled slice across k runs and gated with a tolerance band, would have shown the drop and failed the CI gate even though aggregate accuracy barely moved - exactly the signal the old flat-average eval missed.
